source.title: Scaling up Masked Diffusion Models on Text
source.authors: Shen Nie; Fengqi Zhu; Chao Du; Tianyu Pang; Qian Liu; Guang-Tao Zeng; Min Lin; Chong-Xuan Li

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study extends scaling-law analysis to masked diffusion language models and reports results on their validation-loss and compute-scaling behavior.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the IsoFLOP scaling results and the reported downstream-task trend against validation loss. CFG ablations, conditional-generation results, benchmark comparisons not tied to scaling, and reverse-curse and temporal-shift results do not test these claim versions and are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own IsoFLOP sweeps (6e18 to 1e20 FLOPs) for masked diffusion LMs and matched autoregressive LMs on SlimPajama. It fits loss-vs-compute and optimal-size-vs-compute power laws and relates downstream accuracy to validation loss. These results bear directly on V1, V3 and V6 in a new model class.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that MDM optimal validation loss and optimal model size both follow power laws in compute. The loss rate matches ARMs, with a constant 16x compute gap (smaller than the 64x reported for continuous diffusion), and optimal MDM size is about half the ARM size. They read this as strong scalability, while noting the gap to ARMs as a limitation.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a standard IsoFLOP allocation analysis and compute-loss fit, but applies them to masked diffusion models with a bidirectional Transformer encoder and the MDM validation-loss objective rather than to autoregressive models.

fits_no_version.finding: Changing the training objective (masked diffusion vs autoregressive) leaves the loss-compute exponent similar but shifts the constant. MDMs need about 16x more compute for equal loss, and their compute-optimal size is about half that of ARMs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The training objective or model family shifts the scaling-law constant and the compute-optimal size while preserving the exponent.

record.problems: The compute sweep spans 6 × 10^18 to 10^20 FLOPs, and plotted values and fitted exponents are not reported numerically in the text. The paper says 128 Monte Carlo samples reduce validation-loss estimation variance but reports no uncertainty intervals or error bars for the scaling results.

untested.parts: Loss scaling in parameters or tokens separately with the other non-bottlenecked. Only about 1.2 orders of magnitude of compute (6e18 to 1e20), not several.
No test of whether small-run fits predict much larger runs. The 1.1B models at 1.6e21 and 3.3e21 FLOPs are not compared against the fitted law.
No fitted exponents for N or D. No test of whether N and D grow equally or N faster; D is only implied via C=6ND.
Table 8 varies depth and width, but the effect of shape at fixed N is not analysed.
No other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer scaling.
No comparison of fitting methods, parameter counting, schedules or data. No test for curvature away from a single power law.

missing.what: ARMs and MDMs from the scaling sweep perform near random guessing on ARC-c, WinoGrande and MMLU.

record.verdict_notes: Neither original source; this is a new-setting test in text LMs with a different objective. Arguably this also touches V5 as a 'different training regime', but it is still text pretraining, so it is linked to V1/V3. The record's V1 limits_scope label, based on the narrow compute range, was dropped: an untested range is not a limitation and is listed under untested instead. No exponents, numeric fits or error bars are reported.

versions.untested_parts: Tests validation loss against compute for IsoFLOP-optimal allocations, not independent loss scaling with parameters or tokens while holding the other quantities non-bottlenecking. The tested compute range is 6 × 10^18 to 10^20 FLOPs, not several orders of magnitude.
No test of whether laws fitted on small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
Reports a power-law trend for optimal model size with compute, but does not report a corresponding fitted trend for optimal token count or establish how the parameter and token exponents compare.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No scaling-law test in other modalities or of repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer regimes.
The downstream scaling analysis is limited to language-understanding tasks and does not test broader downstream task families.
No systematic comparison of fitting choices, parameter-counting conventions, data, or schedules, and no test of curves bending away from a single power law.
